items.stem: In Amazon EKS, who is responsible for managing the Kubernetes control plane?

options.text: AWS manages the control plane; you manage worker nodes and workloads
options.rationale: Correct: EKS runs and scales the control plane for you under the shared responsibility model.

options.text: You install and patch the control plane on your own EC2 instances
options.rationale: EKS manages the control plane; you do not run it yourself.
That is not how EKS works.

options.text: It is fully serverless with no worker nodes ever
options.rationale: Workloads still need nodes or Fargate profiles.

items.explanation: Correct: EKS runs and scales the control plane for you under the shared responsibility model.

items.stem: What is the recommended way to give a specific pod permission to read an S3 bucket?

options.rationale: Correct: IRSA scopes AWS permissions to a pod's service account rather than the whole node.

options.text: Attach the policy to the node instance role
options.rationale: That grants the permission to every pod on the node, violating least privilege.

options.text: Hard-code access keys in the pod spec
options.rationale: Static keys in specs are insecure.
Public buckets expose data broadly and do not scope pod access.

items.explanation: Correct: IRSA scopes AWS permissions to a pod's service account rather than the whole node.

items.stem: Which TWO components help a workload scale and stay available on EKS? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A node autoscaler such as Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter
options.rationale: Correct: a node autoscaler adds capacity when pods cannot be scheduled.

options.text: A PodDisruptionBudget to limit voluntary disruptions
options.rationale: Correct: a PDB keeps a minimum number of pods available during disruptions.

options.text: Making all pods use the same node

items.explanation: Correct: a node autoscaler and a PodDisruptionBudget both support scaling and availability.
